help.blenderStep2: Open a Dope Sheet editor and switch to Action Editor mode.
help.blenderStep3: Click the Browse Action menu (the icon to the left of the name) and choose walk / run / etc.
help.blenderAlt: Alternatively use the Nonlinear Animation (NLA) editor: there you'll find all the actions ready to drag.

help.title: Voxel AI Artist guide
help.s.start.b:
The left sidebar has four tabs: *Generate* (AI), *View* (appearance), *Draw* (tools), *Rig* (skeleton and animations).
The right panel lists the scene *objects* and shows their *properties*.
The top bar holds *File* (.voxai projects), *Import*, *Export*, *Help* and *Settings*.
To start from scratch: *Generate > New project*, then pick a name and a grid (e.g. 32,32,32).
Autosave is on: *File > Save history* brings back recent versions.
help.s.nav.b:
*Middle mouse held* orbits the view around the model (like Blender).
*Shift + middle mouse* pans the view; the *wheel* zooms.
The left button stays free for the tools: you don't have to hold anything to draw.
In *View* you can switch on the grid, wireframe, voxel gap and auto-rotation (object or camera).
The scene is redrawn only when something changes, so a still frame counter is normal.
help.s.draw.b:
Tools: [1] View, [2] Place, [3] Remove, [4] Draw (continuous stroke), [5] Pick colour.
The active colour comes from the palette or the picker; *Pick* copies the colour of an existing voxel.
The brush goes from 1 to 6 voxels: [ and ] shrink or grow it.
Green preview = where the voxel will appear; red outline = what will be removed.
[Ctrl+Z] undoes, [Ctrl+Y] (or [Ctrl+Shift+Z]) redoes.
*Clear all* empties the active object's voxels (and its skeleton) after a confirmation.
help.s.sym.b:
*Symmetry* on X/Y/Z mirrors every edit across the grid centre; the translucent plane shows where.
Dragging with the left button selects a *rectangle* of voxels: on release the operation applies to the whole area.
[Q] cycles the drag constraint axis: auto (face normal), X, Y, Z.
[E] arms *extrusion* of the face under the cursor: move the mouse for the thickness, [E] again cycles the axis, [Esc] cancels.
While dragging a rectangle, [E] gives the selection depth: rectangle to block.
help.s.objects.b:
[Tab] switches between *Object mode* (move and select whole objects) and *Edit mode* (work on voxels).
In the Objects panel: *New*, *Duplicate*, *Delete*, *Merge*; the eye hides, double click renames.
*Properties* applies position, rotation (90° steps) and scale live: the value is baked into the voxels when you leave the field.
Every object carries *its own* rig: importing a file into a non-empty scene adds an object instead of replacing the scene.
Note: New / Duplicate / Delete / Merge cannot be undone with [Ctrl+Z].
help.s.ai.b:
In *Generate* describe the model ("a red dragon in a 32 grid") and press Generate.
In *Modify* mode the current model is sent along with your request ("add wings") and the edited version comes back.
The grid goes up to 512 per side; the *big structure* option pushes the AI to use the whole space with facades, interiors, roofs and stairs.
The *Humanoid character* switch enforces T-pose, separated legs and one part per limb, so the model is animatable as soon as it is generated (see the dedicated section).
A valid Gemini session is required: cookies are pasted in *Settings* and never leave your computer.
Malformed answers are repaired automatically; if one stays invalid, retry or rephrase the request.
An automatic voxel cap stops a single bad instruction from filling millions of cells and freezing the app.
help.s.humanoid.b:
In *Generate* there is a *Humanoid character* switch: turn it on when the subject is a person, an anthropomorphic robot or a biped creature.
With it on, the AI gets extra rules: *T-pose*, horizontal arms, straight parallel legs, feet on the ground and the model centred on the X axis.
A *gap of at least 2 voxels* is left between the legs all the way down, and at least 1 voxel under the armpit: without a gap the rig cannot tell the limbs apart.
The most important rule is the *split per limb*: the model comes divided into testa, collo, torso, bacino, braccio_R, mano_R, braccio_L, mano_L, gamba_R, piede_R, gamba_L, piede_L.
The *_R* suffix marks the side at higher X, *_L* the side at lower X: the same convention the app's own skeleton uses.
Clothes and accessories follow the limb they cover: the right trouser leg goes inside *gamba_R*, the right boot inside *piede_R*, hair and helmets inside *testa*.
Parts like *trousers*, *boots*, *gloves* or *dress* are forbidden: they span two limbs, and the rig binds each part to a single bone chain. The result would be one leg with the other welded onto it.
Accessories that do not follow a limb (cape, backpack, tail, wings) stay in parts of their own.
No body part is 1 voxel thick: arms and legs at least 3x3 in section, neck at least 2x2, so the rig has volume to deform.
The switch *turns on the part split by itself* (it clears "single object"): without the parts format the limb names would have nowhere to live.
The *Pack* tab has the same switch, to generate a whole set of consistent, rig-ready characters.
It applies to imported models too: if you split the parts with these names yourself, *Generate skeleton* binds every limb to the right chain.
help.s.pack.b:
A *pack* generates several objects (with variants) in one session, keeping a single style.
The queue lives in the Python process: you can reload the window without losing a long run.
The style is *enforced*, not requested: the palette of the references (or of the first successful asset) is reapplied to all the others.
One request at a time, on purpose: the Gemini client uses browser cookies and would be rate-limited in parallel.
Finished packs stay on disk and export as a single ZIP file.
help.s.rig.b:
*Generate skeleton* builds bones scaled to the model and assigns every voxel to a bone.
If the model is split into parts, each part ends up on *a single bone chain*: a part covering two limbs (like "trousers") welds them together. Generate characters with the *Humanoid character* switch, or split the parts per limb.
To select a joint, click its *light dot*: the search runs in screen pixels, so you don't need to aim precisely.
Gizmo: [R] rotates the bone (pose), [G] moves the joint (to fix the skeleton).
The tip bones of hands, feet and head are hidden: they only give orientation in Blender and take no voxels.
*Show rig* re-enters the preview of the rig already stored on the object, without regenerating it (which would lose pose and weights).
The rig survives rebuilds, object switching and saving: you don't need the Rig tab open to export it.
Bones: *+ Bone* adds a child to the selected one, *double-click the name* renames it, *Delete* reparents its children. The name is the identity: pose, painted weights and clips follow it.
*X symmetry* mirrors the pose in one click (L>R, R>L or swap both sides) and, if you painted weights, the overrides too: the twin voxel is minX+maxX-x.
*Symmetrise skeleton* makes L and R match again after fixes with [G]: it copies one side onto the other (or averages them) and snaps centre bones back to the axis.
*Aim limb (IK)*: turn it on and drag a hand or a foot; the two bones upstream (shoulder+elbow, hip+knee) orient themselves, and a whole drag undoes with a single [Ctrl+Z].
*Pose library*: save the current pose and reapply it even on another object; it lands on bones with the same name, the others are ignored.
help.s.weights.b:
The binding is *rigid*: each voxel belongs to exactly one bone. If a part moves with the wrong bone, repaint it.
Turning on *Weight paint* zeroes the pose (the rest pose is required) and disables the gizmo.
Pick the target bone, then drag over the model with the left button: the colours show each voxel's bone.
Modes: *Brush* (sphere with adjustable radius), *Fill* (all connected voxels sharing the same bone), *Erase* (back to automatic).
*Reset corrections* redoes the automatic binding; every stroke can be undone with [Ctrl+Z].
Corrections are saved in the project and end up in the GLB export.
help.s.anim.b:
Ready-made clips (idle, walk, wave...) are chosen from the menu and play immediately in the preview.
You can ask the AI for an animation: generated clips stay in the rig and are saved with the project.
The pose sliders move the selected bone; the current pose goes into the GLB export.
Playback stops by itself when you enter weight painting, which needs the rest pose.
help.s.export.b:
*GLB* is the format for Blender / Unity / Godot: it carries skeleton, rigid weights and clips. The 1/100 autoscale avoids giant models.
*OBJ + MTL*: coplanar faces are merged into large quads; keep both files in the same folder or materials show up white.
*.vox* for MagicaVoxel, *.schem* for Minecraft (WorldEdit / Litematica).
*.voxelai* (obfuscated) and *.json* (plain) keep everything: voxels, objects, transforms and one rig per object.
The saved rig contains type, bones, pose, painted weights and AI animations: reopening the file restores the same state.
*File > Save project* (.voxai) is the handiest way to pick the work up later.
help.s.keys.b:
[1] [2] [3] [4] [5] tools — [ and ] brush size.
[Tab] Object / Edit mode — [Q] constraint axis — [E] extrusion — [Esc] cancels the current gesture.
[Ctrl+Z] undo — [Ctrl+Y] redo — [Del] deletes the selected object.
[R] and [G] switch the rig gizmo: rotate the pose / move the joint.
[F1] opens this guide. Keys can be reassigned in *Settings > Shortcuts*.
